text: Chapter four moves from pipelines that merely run to pipelines that actually protect production. At Northbridge Retail, "it worked on my laptop" used to be the whole testing story. This lesson turns testing into a gate a machine checks, not something a person has to remember.

Most real test suites are three kinds of test, in increasing cost. Unit tests check one function in isolation, and hundreds can run in seconds. Integration tests check how pieces work together, often against a real database. End-to-end tests drive the whole app like a user would, and there are only a few, because they're slow. A good pipeline runs them in that order and stops at the first failure.

Here's the real job Northbridge Retail runs on every pull request to storefront-api: checkout, set up Python, install dependencies, then unit tests before integration tests. Pytest's exit code is the whole story — zero means every test passed, anything else fails the step, and maxfail=1 stops the unit suite at the first failure instead of grinding through hundreds of tests likely to fail for the same reason.

Once that workflow runs, its result attaches directly to the commit — a small colored icon next to the commit message that's green for passing, red for failing, so nobody has to open the Actions tab just to check.
On a pull request specifically, the Checks tab rolls every job from every workflow into one summary, so a reviewer can see the test job passed before ever opening the Files changed tab.
Tests catch broken behavior. They don't catch style problems, risky patterns, or code nobody's running yet — those are different kinds of risk entirely. That's next, in static analysis and linting.
